review.limitations: Selected technical sections and examples were reviewed. The detailed classification of indeterminacy was read for context, not independently proved.

evidence.description: Distinguishes shape operations from ordinary set operations on their stored elements.
Shared-transform replacement, chevron examples and finite/infinite placement issues.

sections.title: In brief
sections.text: Stiny develops a common algebraic language for drawings, models and symbolic descriptions. It explains why shapes can have recognizable parts that are absent from their stored list of maximal elements.

sections.title: The question
sections.text: How can one computational formalism work across different geometric dimensions and connect spatial and symbolic descriptions without fixing every possible part in advance?

sections.title: Main idea or claim
sections.text: Part relations, sum, difference and transformations organize shape computation. Products of suitable algebras can coordinate descriptions while embedding permits parts to be recognized anew during a derivation.

sections.title: How the work approaches it
sections.text: The paper develops straight-line examples, generalizes by element and ambient dimension, introduces labels and decompositions, and states the rule mechanism through matching followed by transformed replacement.

sections.title: Evidence and examples
sections.text: Two-square and chevron constructions show the difference between stored elements and emergent parts. Other examples examine how extra points can constrain a rule and how configurations can leave infinitely many placements.

sections.title: What comes out of it
sections.text: A unique maximal-element representation does not force a unique interpretation into parts. Coordinates and labels can restrict a computation, but the geometry can still support alternative readings under other rules.

sections.title: Limits to keep in mind
sections.text: Different algebras have different properties and recognition conditions. The paper’s broad cross-domain promise is conceptual, not a demonstrated general software system or a benchmark establishing practical speed.

sections.title: What to take from it
sections.text: Do not equate a set of maximal segments with the set of all meaningful parts. Use the algebra’s geometric operations, then state explicitly which labels or product components constrain the rules.
